newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan PM dangles tax cuts before businessmen.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan PM dangles tax cuts before businessmen.

text.p: Pakistan's new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, outlining an economic strategy of self-reliance, told businessmen on Wednesday he was ready to cut taxes if they promised not to evade them.

In a speech to about 400 invited Pakistani business leaders, he appealed for cooperation in the implementation of his economic agenda, which he said aimed to promote self-reliance, cut the budget deficit and reduce foreign debt.

Sharif said he wanted to slash taxes to encourage people to pay willingly. "You tell me what you can pay and what you cannot pay," the pro-business prime minister said at his first meeting with the business community since his Pakistan Muslim League party's landslide victory in February 3 elections.

"I am prepared to remove what you really cannot pay. But you must pay what you can pay," Sharif said to loud applause. "I want to place blind faith in you and I also expect you to have blind faith in me and deposit your taxes."

Sharif has said his top priority is to revive the ailing economy and stimulate growth and blames Benazir Bhutto's three-year government, dismissed in November on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, for neglecting industry.
Businessmen staged strikes against Bhutto's government to protest at heavy taxes imposed in the June budget for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).
Sharif promised to accept all the business community's genuine demands and revamp the system if it blocked progress.

"We will rectify the mistakes of the past and correct mistakes in the system if there is room for that. But if this cannot be done in the existing system, then we will scrap it and bring a new system," the 47-year-old industrialist declared.
He said his government, with a more than two-thirds majority in parliament, could offer constitutional guarantees if needed.
He proposed that the businessmen form working groups to make recommendations within 10 to 15 days.
Sharif said his government would strive to enable Pakistan to stand on its feet.
"We will live within our means to reach the goal of self-reliance. We will reduce the budget deficit to reduce dependence on domestic and foreign loans," he said.
He said his government would cut public spending in the interest of "domestic self-reliance", widen the tax base and speed up privatisation of state-owned concerns.

"To achieve self-reliance on the external level, we will reduce our trade deficit as much as possible to correct the balance of payments. For this, promotion of exports will be a basic factor in our economic strategy."
Sharif said he would personally review Pakistan's export performance every month.

He did not mention the International Monetary Fund, which wants the government to cut this year's budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from 6.3 percent in 1995/96 as a condition for its current standby loan to Pakistan.
